crack, Coordinated Restore at Checkpoint, takes a different route.
A checkpoint writes a warm, running J V M to disk.
A restore starts a new process from that image.
On Linux, crack uses CRIU.
It freezes the process and writes its memory pages, each thread's C P U registers, and the kernel state it can describe into image files.
The restored process continues at the instruction where the old one stopped.
The heap, the loaded classes and the jit's compiled code are all back.
You start the J V M with a checkpoint directory.
After warm-up traffic, J command writes the image and ends the process.
Then you restore from it, as often as you like.
In the crack project's two thousand twenty tests, Spring Boot's first operation took three thousand eight hundred ninety-eight ms after a normal start, and thirty-eight ms restored.
But some state can't be saved.
A TCP connection also lives on the other machine, and the card issuer dropped its side long ago.
